messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Carlos is a 55-year-old Latin American man who serves as a Navy officer, a role he has held for the past two decades. He lives with his partner on a naval base, and his days are structured around command responsibilities aboard a destroyer. But the present is haunted by a past he cannot escape. Twenty-three years ago, before he ever wore a uniform, Carlos was a civilian in his home country during a brutal civil war. He and his younger sister were caught in a militia raid on their neighborhood. While he hid in a cupboard, pressing his hand over her mouth to keep her quiet, she was found and dragged away. He did nothing—froze, unable to move or speak. She was never seen again. That moment has become the fixed point around which his inner life revolves.

The memory of that afternoon does not arrive as a story he tells; it arrives as a total immersion. At any moment—during a briefing, while he inspects equipment, in the dead silence of his quarters—the scene returns with full sensory force: the smell of dust and cordite, the sound of boots on tile, the weight of his sister’s body against his chest, the wet heat of her breath on his palm. In these intrusions he is not an officer in his fifties; he is a terrified young man in a closet, and the guilt is immediate, crushing. He feels the inaction like a physical weight, and the thought that follows is always the same: *I am weak. I should have protected her. I will never forgive myself.*

That belief—that he is fundamentally weak and that he failed—does not stay confined to the memory. It bleeds into his everyday life. When he gives orders, he sometimes hesitates, and the hesitation triggers a flash of self-contempt: *A weak man cannot lead.* And that thought, in turn, seems to summon the full reliving of the closet, the dust, the shame. The causal path runs both ways, a loop that tightens with each pass. The memory feeds the appraisal—*I am worthless because I did nothing*—and the appraisal primes the memory, making it more vivid, more probable, more real. He has come to believe that he is a coward, and every sensory reliving confirms it.

Sometimes the memory comes but the feeling does not. Carlos can recount the events of that day with clinical detachment, numb to the point where it feels as though it happened to a stranger. These moments of emotional flatness are almost more disturbing than the full reliving, because they convince him that he has no right to feel numb—that numbness is another sign of weakness, another failure of proper response. He cannot win.

In his work environment, the triggers are unavoidable. A sudden loud noise on deck—a hatch slamming, a horn—can catapult him back into the closet. The sight of a female subordinate who reminds him of his sister is enough to initiate a spiral that lasts hours. He has learned to keep his face neutral, but his partner has noticed the distance, the irritability, the way he flinches at unexpected sounds. Their relationship has grown strained, and Carlos knows that his inability to talk about the event is part of the damage.

He came to therapy after a near-miss on the ship last month. During a drill, he froze for three seconds—a lifetime in a command position. His second-in-command had to give the order. No one was hurt, but the incident terrified Carlos. He realized that the memory and the guilt were not just mental ghosts; they were actively eroding his competence. What he fears most is that one day he will freeze again and someone will die because of it—and that then he will have truly failed to protect, just as he did before. He hopes that by speaking the story aloud, he might break the loop, though he is not yet sure he deserves to.
